title: Linked Lists
summary: A linked list is a chain of nodes on the heap, each holding a value and a pointer to the next, ending in NULL. Adding at the front is instant and nothing ever has to move, but finding the nth element means walking the chain. Inserting and removing use a pointer to the link being changed, and freeing the list walks it once.

cards.q: How does the last node of a linked list mark the end?
cards.a:
Its next pointer is NULL

Loops stop when they reach NULL.

cards.q: Why does push_front take struct node **head?
cards.a:
It must change the caller's head pointer

The same idea as swap(int *, int *).

cards.q: In free_list, why save head->next before calling free(head)?
cards.a:
After free, reading head->next is a use after free

Freed memory is no longer yours.

cards.q: Which is faster on a linked list than on an array?
cards.a:
Inserting at the front

Arrays win at access by index and at walking through memory.
